conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot anything from routine “baby blues” to signs of depression or anxiety that deserve extra support. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinicians who need to know to keep you safe. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to hear your honest experience. Ready to start?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—maybe when the baby did something silly or during everyday moments?

Hi Sarah. I... yeah, I guess I can still laugh sometimes. When my little guy sneezes he makes this tiny squeak and my husband and I both crack up. But it feels kind of muted—like I have to remind myself to enjoy it instead of it just happening naturally. Most of the time I’m too tired or preoccupied to find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I’ve been able to laugh, but it doesn’t come as easily. I still smile when the baby does something cute, yet it feels kind of forced—like I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment instead of worrying about whether he’s breathing okay or if I’m doing everything right.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some stuff—like my mom coming over so I can shower in peace or the little walk we sometimes take around the block—but the excitement feels kind of dim. Mostly I’m just hoping nothing goes wrong while we’re out.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday he spit up a ton after I fed him and I immediately thought, “Great, I must’ve over-fed him or held him wrong.” I know rationally it’s normal, but the thought still pops in that I should’ve figured it out better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Um… yeah, pretty much every day. Like, I’ll be sitting on the couch and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure his breathing sounds different, even though it’s probably fine. Or I’ll worry the bottle temp was wrong and he’ll get a stomachache. I know it’s probably “no good reason,” but in the moment it feels huge.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had full-on panic, but I do get these sudden waves of fear—like last night I woke up absolutely convinced something was wrong with him, even though he was sleeping peacefully. My chest got tight and I couldn’t settle back down for a while. It passes, but it’s scary when it hits.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days it feels like I’m treading water. I’ll finally get him down for a nap and realize I haven’t eaten or the laundry’s piled up, and suddenly I’m on the verge of tears because it all seems like too much. I manage, but it’s exhausting—like I’m always one step behind.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m “so unhappy,” but I do have trouble sleeping. My mind keeps spinning—did I sterilize the bottles right, is he gaining enough weight, will he wake up the second I drift off? It takes me forever to settle, and I wake up at every little sound he makes.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—like this heavy, foggy feeling—but it’s not all day, every day. It kind of sneaks up in the late afternoon when I’m most tired, or when I’m feeding him alone at 3 a.m. The rest of the time I just feel flat, neither happy nor really miserable.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No… I haven’t cried much this week—maybe once, when I couldn’t get him to latch in the middle of the night and felt like a lousy mom. Mostly the tears just sit behind my eyes but don’t spill over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤3 mo post-delivery (per self-report)

Presenting symptoms endorsed:
- Anhedonia / diminished enjoyment (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame (Q3)  
- Persistent, intrusive worry and physiological arousal (Q4, Q5)  
- Overwhelm and sense of “treading water” (Q6)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to ruminative worry (Q7)  
- Intermittent sad or “flat” mood, worse late afternoon/night (Q8)  
- Occasional tearfulness but no daily crying spells (Q9)

Patterns:
- Symptoms present most days, fluctuate with fatigue and infant-care demands  
- Anxiety features (racing heart, catastrophic thoughts about infant safety) as prominent as mood symptoms  
- Functional impact: difficulty resting during infant sleep periods, chores piling up, feels “one step behind”

Screening significance:
Meets clinical threshold for at least probable minor-to-moderate postpartum depression with prominent comorbid anxiety; does not endorse anhedonia or low mood of full-day duration every day, so severity likely below major depressive episode level at present.  
No self-harm ideation, intent, or plan reported (Q10) – safety risk absent at screening.

Risk factors documented:
- Primiparous, sleep deprivation, high self-expectations, limited respite  
- Absence of suicidal ideation; protective factor: strong infant-focused motivation

Recommend follow-up:
Structured diagnostic interview (e.g., EPDS, PHQ-9/GAD-7), psychoeducation, and consideration of referral to perinatal mental-health specialty services for further evaluation and support.
